newsitem.title: USA: Battle for Congress hotly contested in West.
newsitem.headline: Battle for Congress hotly contested in West.

text.p: With President Clinton far ahead in the polls and attention shifting to the battle for control of Congress, the outcome of Senate races in the Rocky Mountain states is expected to be crucial.

Colorado, Wyoming and Idaho, although small in population, could play a major role Tuesday in deciding whether Democrats retake the Senate or Republicans maintain the majority they won two years ago, political analysts say.

There are now 53 Republicans and 47 Democrats in the Senate, meaning the Democrats need to capture only three more seats if Clinton is re-elected. Vice President Al Gore votes in the Senate in the case of a tie.

In Colorado, where Republican Representative Wayne Allard faces Democrat Tom Strickland for the seat being vacated by Republican Hank Brown after one term, the race is tight. "It's too close to call," political consultant Eric Sondermann said.
Strickland had actor Robert Redford campaigning for him in Denver, but Allard has an important plus -- the endorsement of Denver's two major newspapers, the Rocky Mountain News and The Denver Post.

Strickland, an attorney and lobbyist, is running for office for the first time. Allard, who was a veterinarian before going into the House of Representatives, has made much of Strickland's past work as a lobbyist.

Sondermann expects abortion to remain on the front burner in Strickland's campaign advertising and in the past few days Strickland, who favours abortion rights, has highlighted his position in his TV ads. Allard opposes abortion rights.

A question that remains unanswered is what type of "coattail effect" a victorious Clinton might have on other races. Clinton and Republican challenger Bob Dole, in a close race for Colorado's eight electoral votes, have visited Colorado more than would be expected for a state its size.
Voters who want to see Congress remain Republican could play a key role in Senate races, Sondermann said. If even only five percent split their vote it could determine the results.

Abortion is not a hot issue in neighbouring Wyoming where Republican state senator Mike Enzi faces Democrat Kathy Karpan, a former two-term secretary of state, for the seat being vacated by three-term Republican Sen. Alan Simpson.

Wyoming has not had a Democratic U.S. senator since Gale McGee lost his election for a fourth term in 1976 and Enzi leads by several percentage points in polls, but the race is statistically a dead heat.

Ron Faucheux, editor of Campaigns & Elections monthly magazine, noted that Wyoming is a Republican-dominated state but Karpan's popularity as a vote getter has kept the race tight. She lost her bid for governor in 1994, caught in a wave of anti-Clinton sentiment.

Land use has become the key issue, James King, associate professor of political science at the University of Wyoming, said. Karpan reminds voters that when she was Wyoming secretary of state and on a land use commission she voted for a moratorium on the sale of lands put in trust for education.

Enzi, as a state legislator, voted against the moratorium once and for it on a second vote. But Karpan has gone on the offensive on an issue that puts environmentalists and hunters in the same camp -- preserving open space. Both candidates have an "A" rating from the National Rifle Association.

In Oregon, where Republican Mark Hatfield is retiring after 30 years, Democrat Tom Bruggere, a self-made computer-software millionaire, faces Republican Gordon Smith, a frozen-food mogul. The race is considered statistically too close to call.
